name: Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria
aliases: Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella infections

clinicalPearls: HACEK is an acronym for a group of fastidious, slow-growing gram-negative bacteria that require a carbon-dioxide-enriched atmosphere and do not grow on routine enteric media such as MacConkey agar: Haemophilus species, Aggregatibacter (formerly Actinobacillus) species, Cardiobacterium species, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella kingae.

These organisms normally colonize the oral cavity; invasive disease characteristically follows a recent dental procedure or nasopharyngeal infection in a patient with underlying valvular heart disease or prosthetic valves.

A positive HACEK blood culture is strongly predictive of underlying infective endocarditis, with an overall positive predictive value around 60%, though this varies sharply by organism (e.g., 62-100% with Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans bacteremia versus only 0-6% with Eikenella bacteremia).

HACEK organisms cause roughly 0.8-6% of infective endocarditis cases, most often due to Aggregatibacter species, Haemophilus species, and Cardiobacterium hominis; the aortic and mitral valves are most commonly affected.

Compared with non-HACEK endocarditis, HACEK endocarditis occurs in younger patients and is more frequently associated with embolic, vascular, and immunologic manifestations; systemic embolization is common (major emboli in roughly 28-71% of cases) and vegetations are seen on echocardiography in up to 85% of patients.

Kingella kingae behaves differently from the other HACEK organisms: more than half of K. kingae infections are bone and joint infections, oropharyngeal colonization peaks in the first 3 years of life and is higher in daycare-attending children, and it can be transmitted child-to-child and cause outbreaks; K. kingae bacteremia can present with a petechial rash resembling Neisseria meningitidis sepsis.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus and C. cynodegmi are endogenous to the dog and cat mouth; infection often follows a dog or cat bite (or exposure without a bite), and asplenia, glucocorticoid use, and alcohol abuse predispose to severe sepsis with shock and DIC, classically with a petechial rash progressing to purpura and gangrene.

Pasteurella multocida colonizes the respiratory and GI tracts of domestic animals (oropharyngeal colonization 50-90% in cats, 50-70% in dogs) and is transmitted by bites, scratches, or licking; most human infections are skin and soft tissue, and almost two-thirds are caused by cats.

Aeromonas can produce ecthyma gangrenosum (hemorrhagic vesicles with a rim of erythema and central necrosis/ulceration) resembling lesions of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, and is associated with water exposure, floods, and other hydrologic disasters (along with Shewanella and Chromobacterium).

Diagnostic recovery of HACEK organisms is improved by alerting the microbiology laboratory; most cultures turn positive within the first week with modern systems (e.g., BACTEC), and prolonged incubation has not been shown to increase recovery of clinically significant isolates.

Molecular methods aid diagnosis: 16S rRNA gene amplification (PCR) on blood or cardiac valve tissue and MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry on colonies increase the accuracy and speed of HACEK identification; real-time PCR and inoculation of synovial fluid into aerobic blood culture bottles enhance recovery of K. kingae in culture-negative cases.

Chromobacterium violaceum causes rare but often fatal soft tissue infections and metastatic abscesses, occurring especially in children with defective neutrophil function such as chronic granulomatous disease.
harrison.pathophysiology: HACEK organisms are commensals of the human oral cavity. Disruption of the oral mucosa (dental procedures, nasopharyngeal infection, periodontal disease) allows transient bacteremia; in patients with damaged native valves or prosthetic material, the slow-growing organisms seed and form valvular vegetations, producing a typically subacute, indolent endocarditis. Their fastidious, CO2-dependent slow growth accounts for delayed culture positivity and difficulty in susceptibility testing (including underdetection of beta-lactamase). The remaining fastidious and miscellaneous gram-negative organisms in this chapter act largely as opportunists: animal-mouth flora (Pasteurella multocida, Capnocytophaga canimorsus) inoculated through bites/scratches/licking, environmental and waterborne organisms (Aeromonas, Shewanella, Chromobacterium violaceum, Achromobacter xylosoxidans) introduced through wounds or contaminated fluids, and nosocomial nonfermenters (Elizabethkingia/Chryseobacterium, Rhizobium radiobacter, Alcaligenes faecalis) associated with contaminated fluids, indwelling devices, and immunocompromised hosts.
additionalDifferentials: Viridans group streptococcal endocarditis (also subacute, culture-positive, common in dental-source disease)
Culture-negative endocarditis (Bartonella, Coxiella burnetii, Tropheryma whipplei) when blood cultures are sterile
Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis when the course is more acute
Septic arthritis/osteomyelitis from Staphylococcus aureus in children (where K. kingae may have surpassed S. aureus as a leading cause)
Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection when ecthyma gangrenosum-like skin lesions are present (Aeromonas)
infectionMimics: Neisseria meningitidis sepsis (K. kingae bacteremia can produce a similar petechial rash)
Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection (Aeromonas can cause indistinguishable ecthyma gangrenosum)
Other gram-negative bacteremic pneumonias (Achromobacter xylosoxidans bacteremia, similar high mortality)
Other causes of culture-negative or slow-growing endocarditis
nonInfectiousMimics: Noninfective embolic disease and vasculitis (HACEK endocarditis frequently presents with embolic, vascular, and immunologic phenomena such as cerebrovascular accidents, mycotic aneurysms, and immune-complex glomerulonephritis that may mimic primary vasculitic or thromboembolic disorders)
Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (rare HUS following bloody diarrhea has been linked to Aeromonas, but HUS itself is the differential)
additionalInvestigations: Blood cultures with notification of the laboratory that a HACEK organism is suspected; modern automated systems (e.g., BACTEC) usually yield growth within the first week
16S rRNA gene amplification (PCR) of blood or cardiac valve specimens for culture-negative or fastidious cases
MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry performed directly on colonies for rapid, accurate species identification
Echocardiography to detect valvular vegetations (seen in up to 85% of HACEK endocarditis)
Real-time PCR of blood or joint fluid for Kingella kingae; inoculation of synovial fluid into aerobic blood culture bottles to improve recovery

In vitro antimicrobial susceptibility testing, including Etest, given slow growth and possible undetected beta-lactamase; susceptibility testing is essential for the miscellaneous multidrug-resistant gram-negative organisms
redFlags: Systemic embolization (cerebral and other major emboli are common in HACEK endocarditis)
Congestive heart failure complicating endocarditis (reported in roughly 19-50% of Haemophilus HACEK cases)
Petechial/purpuric rash with sepsis after a dog or cat bite in an asplenic, alcohol-abusing, or glucocorticoid-treated patient (Capnocytophaga canimorsus, may progress to shock, DIC, and gangrene)
Petechial rash with bacteremia mimicking meningococcemia (Kingella kingae)
Necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis after water/wound exposure (Aeromonas; very high mortality with myonecrosis)
Sepsis with metastatic abscesses in a child with defective neutrophil function (Chromobacterium violaceum)
harrison.prognosis: Overall prognosis in both native-valve and prosthetic-valve HACEK endocarditis is excellent and significantly better than endocarditis caused by non-HACEK pathogens; one case-control study found significantly lower 1-year mortality than viridans group streptococcal endocarditis. Mortality associated with HACEK endocarditis in older series ranged from about 28 to 71% depending on the cohort. By contrast, several miscellaneous organisms carry high mortality: Pasteurella multocida invasive disease up to ~30% despite therapy, Achromobacter xylosoxidans bacteremia up to ~67%, Aeromonas sepsis ~25% in immunocompromised adults and >90% with myonecrosis, Chryseobacterium indologenes up to ~50%, and Elizabethkingia anophelis bloodstream infection ~18%.
pitfalls: Because of slow growth, antimicrobial susceptibility testing may be difficult and beta-lactamase production may go undetected; resistance is most common in Haemophilus and Aggregatibacter species.

Prolonged blood-culture incubation has not been shown to improve recovery of clinically significant HACEK isolates, so relying on extended incubation alone may delay diagnosis-molecular methods may be needed.
Failing to alert the microbiology laboratory that a fastidious HACEK organism is suspected can compromise recovery and identification.
Eikenella corrodens is resistant to clindamycin, metronidazole, and aminoglycosides, so empirical regimens chosen for typical gram-negatives may fail.

Many miscellaneous gram-negative organisms (Achromobacter, Elizabethkingia/Chryseobacterium, Chromobacterium, Aeromonas) are frequently multidrug-resistant-Elizabethkingia/Chryseobacterium are typically resistant to carbapenems while Aeromonas can produce carbapenemases-so therapy must be guided by susceptibility testing rather than assumptions.
Capnocytophaga canimorsus infection may be missed when there is exposure without an obvious scratch or bite, and severe disease can occur in patients without an apparent wound.
harrison.severityClassification: No formal grading system; clinical severity is stratified by site and host factors. HACEK endocarditis runs a typically subacute course (more aggressive with Kingella kingae) with severity marked by embolic, vascular, and immunologic complications, heart failure, and mycotic aneurysm. For the miscellaneous organisms, severity escalates with immunocompromise, asplenia, cirrhosis, malignancy, diabetes, neutrophil dysfunction, and extremes of age, and with deep/invasive presentations such as bacteremia, necrotizing fasciitis, myonecrosis, and septic shock with DIC.
